title: Gauge for round work
subtitle: Why the gauge in your flat swatch may not match your round gauge
excerpt: Gauge swatches are normally worked flat. But crochet gauge can shift when you switch from rows to rounds because the yarn-tension hand always works on the same pass. Checking gauge in the round is the only way to be sure of size on hats, bags, and amigurumi.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book — gauge variance in round work. Standard technical crochet references.

glossaryTerms.definition: The stitch and row count per 10 cm when working in continuous rounds or joined rounds. May differ from flat gauge for the same yarn, hook, and stitch pattern.
A small circular or tubular piece worked to check gauge for a project that will be made in rounds. More accurate for hats and tubes than a flat swatch.

heroPrompt: A small flat-worked gauge swatch and a small round tube swatch in the same cream DK cotton side by side on a pale surface, both with a ruler placed across them at the 10 cm mark.

content.text: Most crocheters check gauge on a flat swatch — a square of fabric worked in rows. For flat projects (blankets, scarves, garment panels) this is accurate enough. For

— hats, bags, amigurumi, tubular sleeves — the flat swatch can mislead. Some crocheters work consistently tighter or looser when working in the round, because the yarn-tension hand always passes in the same direction and the unworked side of the fabric is always inside.
How much does round gauge vary?

For some crocheters, not at all — flat and round gauge are identical. For others, the difference is half a stitch per 10 cm, which on a 50 cm hat is significant. If you have finished a hat that came out 3-4 cm too wide or too small on the correct gauge, check your round gauge specifically.
Working a gauge swatch in the round

For a tube: make a foundation chain about 50 cm long, join into a ring, and work in joined rounds or a continuous spiral for 15-20 rounds. Measure across 10 cm of the tube in the middle (not at the first or last few rows).

for a flat-circle item (hat crown, bag base): work a magic ring and the first 8-10 rounds as written, then measure across the widest point and compare to the pattern's schematic measurement for that round count.

If round gauge is tighter than flat gauge: go up half a hook size for round work. If round gauge is looser: go down half a size. Make the adjustment only for the round sections — if a pattern has both flat and round sections, you may use different hooks for each.
